# Are your lien deadlines still open?

> Free calculator for the preliminary notice and lien filing deadlines a subcontractor or supplier faces in California, Texas, Florida, Arizona, Washington, Georgia, Colorado, North Carolina, New York and Ohio. Enter your first and last day on the job; see both dates, weekend flags, and days left. Entirely client-side, nothing uploaded.

Free to use and source available (FSL-1.1-MIT). Results are estimates from the numbers typed in, not legal, tax, financial or professional advice.

## What it covers

- Texas: one notice date per month of unpaid work (15th day of the 3rd month after it, 2nd on residential), lien affidavit 15th of the 4th (3rd) month; rules for original contracts from 2022-01-01, the same for every tier.
- Georgia: Notice to Contractor shown only for second-tier claimants (hired by a subcontractor), as the statute requires it only without privity with the contractor.
- Washington: a subcontractor hired by the prime contractor owes no notice of right to claim a lien (RCW 60.04.031(2)(c)), except on repair or remodel of an existing owner-occupied single-family home; second-tier claimants get the 60-day (10-day on a new single-family home) look-back.
- Late notices: California and Arizona protect work from 20 days before a late notice, Washington 60 (10); Florida treats a late Notice to Owner as a complete defense to the lien (713.06(2)(a)). A passed date shows the earliest work a notice served today still covers.
- Each result links the statute sections it uses; timing checked against the statute text on 2026-11-25 (California's sub lien clock is Civ. Code § 8414).
- California, Arizona, Florida, Colorado, North Carolina, New York: the same clocks for first- and second-tier claimants.
- North Carolina: Notice to Lien Agent 15 days after first furnishing (projects with a designated lien agent); claim of lien 120 days after last furnishing (G.S. 44A-11.2, 44A-12).
- New York: no preliminary notice on private work; notice of lien 8 months after final furnishing, 4 months on a single family dwelling (Lien Law § 10).
- Ohio: notice of furnishing 21 days after first furnishing where a notice of commencement was recorded; affidavit of lien 75 days after last furnishing, 60 on a one- or two-family dwelling (R.C. 1311.05, 1311.06).
- Related: [pay application guides](https://marisstella.app/pay-app-guides/) (schedule of values, retainage, lien waivers).

## Answers

The questions each page answers in its "Common questions" section, with the answer as the page states it. Each link opens that section; the page has the sources.

- [What is a preliminary notice in a mechanics lien claim?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): A preliminary notice (called a Notice to Owner in Florida, a notice of claim for unpaid labor or materials in Texas, and a 20-day preliminary notice in Arizona) is a written notice a subcontractor or supplier sends to the owner and general contractor early in a job, to preserve the right to file a lien later. Several states make it a condition of lien rights, so a missed deadline can cost the claim.
- [How long do I have to file a mechanics lien after finishing the work?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): It depends on the state. California allows 90 days after completion of the project, or 30 days after the owner records a notice of completion. Florida allows 90 days after your last furnishing, Washington 90 days after your last furnishing, Arizona 120 days after completion or 60 days after a recorded notice of completion, and Texas the 15th day of the 4th month on commercial work or the 3rd month on residential work.
- [When does the preliminary notice clock start?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): For California, Arizona, Florida, and Washington it starts on the day you first furnished labor or materials: 20 days in California and Arizona, 45 days in Florida, and 60 days in Washington (10 days on new single-family residential work). Texas instead counts months: the 15th day of the 3rd month after the month of unpaid work on commercial jobs, or the 2nd month on residential jobs.
- [Do I need a separate Texas notice for every month of work?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): Yes. On Texas contracts signed from 2022, each month of unpaid labor or materials has its own notice date: the 15th day of the 3rd month after that month on commercial work, or the 2nd month on residential work. The calculator lists one date per month from your first to your last day on the job.
- [Does it matter whether the general contractor or a subcontractor hired me?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): Among the ten states here it changes the result in Georgia and Washington. Georgia requires a Notice to Contractor only from claimants without a direct contract with the general contractor. Washington exempts a subcontractor hired by the prime contractor from its notice, except on repair or remodel of an existing owner-occupied single-family home (RCW 60.04.031(2)(c), (3)(b)). Texas gives every tier the same notice dates on contracts from 2022; earlier Texas projects had an extra 2nd-month notice for second-tier claimants.
- [Do North Carolina, New York and Ohio need a preliminary notice?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): North Carolina asks for a Notice to Lien Agent within 15 days of first furnishing on projects with a designated lien agent, and the claim of lien is due 120 days after your last furnishing. New York has no preliminary notice on private work; the notice of lien is due 8 months after your final work or materials, or 4 months on a single family dwelling. Ohio asks a subcontractor or supplier for a notice of furnishing within 21 days of first furnishing where a notice of commencement was recorded, and the affidavit of lien is due 75 days after your last furnishing, or 60 days on a one- or two-family home.
- [What happens if I send the preliminary notice late?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): It depends on the state. In California and Arizona a late notice still counts but protects only work furnished in the 20 days before it was given, and everything after (Cal. Civ. Code § 8204, Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-992.01). Washington works the same way with 60 days, or 10 days on a new single-family home (RCW 60.04.031). In Florida a missing or late Notice to Owner is a complete defense to the lien (Fla. Stat. § 713.06(2)(a)). When the date has passed, the calculator gives the earliest work date a notice served today still covers.
- [Why does the calculator use my last furnishing date when I do not know the completion date?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): Some states measure the lien deadline from completion of the whole project. Your own last day on the job can only be the same as or earlier than completion, so using it gives the same date or an earlier, safer one. Entering the real completion date can only move the deadline later.
- [Is this legal advice?](https://marisstella.app/mechanics-lien-deadline-calculator/#faq): No. This tool applies a simplified reading of published state timing rules to the dates you enter, for a subcontractor or supplier hired by the general contractor or by a subcontractor. It does not model third-tier claimants, public projects, required notice content, delivery method, or foreclosure deadlines, and lien rights can be lost by missing a deadline. Confirm every date with a construction attorney or the current statute before relying on it.
